Let $k$ be a field. A **Lie algebra over $k$** is a $k$-vector space
$\mathfrak g$ ([[def-vector-space]]) together with a map

$$[-,-]:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak g$$

that is linear in each variable ([[def-linear-map]]) and satisfies, for all
$x,y,z\in\mathfrak g$,

$$[x,x]=0$$

and

$$[x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0.$$

The first identity is **alternation** and the second is the **Jacobi identity**.
No finite-dimensional hypothesis is imposed. Alternation implies
$[x,y]=-[y,x]$ in every characteristic: expand
$0=[x+y,x+y]=[x,y]+[y,x]$. Thus skew-symmetry is a consequence here, not a
replacement for alternation in characteristic $2$.

The zero vector space, with its unique bracket, is a Lie algebra. A Lie algebra
is **abelian** when $[x,y]=0$ for every $x,y$.

symmetric, invariant bilinear form on it. If
$x_1,\ldots,x_n$ is a basis and $x^1,\ldots,x^n$ is its $B$-dual basis, the
**Casimir element relative to $B$** is

$$\Omega_B=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x^i\in U(\mathfrak g).$$

On a representation $\rho:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$, its **Casimir
operator** is

$$\rho(\Omega_B)=\sum_{i=1}^n\rho(x_i)\rho(x^i).$$

The empty sums give zero when $\mathfrak g=0$. Nondegeneracy is exactly what
identifies $\mathfrak g$ with its dual and supplies the dual basis.
Independence of the chosen basis and commutation with the action are proved in
the next lemma.

The Casimir element $\Omega_B$ is independent of the chosen dual bases and
belongs to the center of $U(\mathfrak g)$. Consequently its action on every
$\mathfrak g$-module is a $\mathfrak g$-intertwiner.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra. Here simple means nonabelian with no ideals except $0$ and $\mathfrak g$, using the Lie and ideal conventions of [[def-finite-semisimple-lie-algebra-and-symmetric-adjoint-action]]. Put $\mathbb C[t,t^{-1}]=\{\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}a_mt^m:a_m\in\mathbb C,\text{ finitely many }a_m\ne0\}$, with multiplication $t^mt^n=t^{m+n}$.

The **algebraic loop algebra** is $L\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[t,t^{-1}]$. Write $x_m=x\otimes t^m$ and define
$$[x\otimes f,y\otimes q]=[x,y]\otimes fq.$$
This is well-defined on the tensor product because the displayed operation is complex bilinear in each tensor's two entries and respects scalar balancing. On three pure tensors its cyclic Jacobi sum is $([x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]])\otimes fqr=0$. Antisymmetry follows from that in $\mathfrak g$ and $fq=qf$. Bilinear and trilinear extension give the identities on all finite sums, including zero. Thus this is a Lie algebra. Only Laurent polynomials occur; no topology or analytic completion is part of the definition.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with
Killing form $B$ ([[def-killing-form-of-a-finite-dimensional-lie-algebra]]). A
**compact real form** of $\mathfrak g$ is a real form $\mathfrak g_0$ of
$\mathfrak g$ ([[def-real-form-of-a-complex-lie-algebra]]) whose Killing form
$B_{\mathfrak g_0}=B|_{\mathfrak g_0\times\mathfrak g_0}$ is **negative
definite**, that is $B(X,X)<0$ for every nonzero $X\in\mathfrak g_0$ and
$B(X,X)=0$ if and only if $X=0$. A real Lie algebra is called **compact** when
its Killing form is negative definite; under this terminology the compact real
forms are exactly the real forms that are compact as real Lie algebras. The
existence and conjugacy of compact real forms are the content of
[[thm-existence-of-a-compact-real-form]] and
[[thm-conjugacy-of-compact-real-forms]].

Use [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]]. Fix the positive-real rescaling $B$ of the Killing form whose induced form on the real finite-root span makes every long root have square $2$. The Killing form is nondegenerate, invariant and symmetric by [[lem-finite-lie-engel-trace-criterion-and-killing-nondegeneracy]], and its restriction gives a positive definite real root form by [[lem-finite-semisimple-cartan-root-and-string-structure]], so this rescaling exists. In particular $B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z])$.

For $f=\sum_m a_mt^m$ put $f'=\sum_m ma_mt^{m-1}$ and $\operatorname{Res}(f\,dt)=a_{-1}$. Define the residue bilinear form by
$$\omega(x\otimes f,y\otimes q)=B(x,y)\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt).$$
The formula is balanced and complex bilinear, so extends uniquely to the tensor product. In particular,
$$\omega(x_m,y_n)=m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y).$$
The Kronecker symbol is one when $m=-n$ and zero otherwise. This form is in fact an alternating Lie-algebra two-cocycle. For Laurent polynomials $f,q$, the residue of $(fq)'$ is zero, so $\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt)=-\operatorname{Res}(fq'\,dt)$; symmetry of $B$ gives skew-symmetry, and in characteristic zero also $\omega(a,a)=0$. For pure tensors $x\otimes f,y\otimes q,z\otimes h$, invariance and symmetry of $B$ make the three factors $B([x,y],z)$, $B([y,z],x)$, and $B([z,x],y)$ equal. The cyclic cocycle sum is therefore that common factor times
$$\operatorname{Res}\bigl(((fq)'h+(qh)'f+(hf)'q)\,dt\bigr)=2\operatorname{Res}((fqh)'\,dt)=0.$$
Trilinearity extends the identity to all loop-algebra elements. Thus the terminology “two-cocycle” records a proved property of the defined form, not merely an intended later use.

For any long root $\alpha$, opposite root vectors normalized by $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=\alpha^\vee$ satisfy
$$B(e_\alpha,f_\alpha)=\frac{2}{(\alpha,\alpha)}=1.$$
The equality follows by pairing $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]$ with the Cartan and using invariance. A later result identifies the highest root and proves that it is long; no highest-root existence claim is used here.

derivations.claim: The adjoint representation is irreducible: an invariant subspace $U\subseteq\mathfrak g$ satisfies $[\mathfrak g,U]\subseteq U$, so it is an ideal, and [F3] leaves only $0$ and $\mathfrak g$. By [F2], $T=\operatorname{ad}(\Omega_B)$ commutes with every $\operatorname{ad}(x)$. Since $T$ is an endomorphism of a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space, it has an eigenvalue $\gamma_B$; its nonzero eigenspace is invariant under $\mathfrak g$, hence is all of $\mathfrak g$. Therefore $T=\gamma_B\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}$, and this scalar is unique.

Choose a $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$-orthonormal basis $X_i$ of $\mathfrak k$. By [F4] and [F5], $Q$ is positive definite and the $B$-dual basis is $-X_i$, so $\Omega_B=-\sum_iX_i^2$. Invariance of $Q$ makes each $\operatorname{ad}(X_i)$ skew-adjoint, and therefore $Q(TX,X)=Q\!\left(-\sum_i[X_i,[X_i,X]],X\right)=\sum_i Q([X_i,X],[X_i,X]).$ For $X\ne0$ this is positive: if it were zero, each $[X_i,X]$ would vanish, so $X$ would be central in $\mathfrak k$ and hence in $\mathfrak g$, contrary to [F3]. Since $T=\gamma_B I$, dividing by $Q(X,X)>0$ shows that $\gamma_B$ is a positive real number.

Thus, for a $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$-orthonormal basis of a compact real form from [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], $-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2=2h^\vee I$; this is the normalization used in the affine central term and every Sugawara denominator below.

Use [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]]. Fix the positive-real rescaling $B$ of the Killing form whose induced form on the real finite-root span makes every long root have square $2$. The Killing form is nondegenerate, invariant and symmetric by [[lem-finite-lie-engel-trace-criterion-and-killing-nondegeneracy]], and its restriction gives a positive definite real root form by [[lem-finite-semisimple-cartan-root-and-string-structure]], so this rescaling exists. In particular $B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z])$.

For $f=\sum_m a_mt^m$ put $f'=\sum_m ma_mt^{m-1}$ and $\operatorname{Res}(f\,dt)=a_{-1}$. Define the residue bilinear form by
$$\omega(x\otimes f,y\otimes q)=B(x,y)\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt).$$
The formula is balanced and complex bilinear, so extends uniquely to the tensor product. In particular,
$$\omega(x_m,y_n)=m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y).$$
The Kronecker symbol is one when $m=-n$ and zero otherwise. This form is in fact an alternating Lie-algebra two-cocycle. For Laurent polynomials $f,q$, the residue of $(fq)'$ is zero, so $\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt)=-\operatorname{Res}(fq'\,dt)$; symmetry of $B$ gives skew-symmetry, and in characteristic zero also $\omega(a,a)=0$. For pure tensors $x\otimes f,y\otimes q,z\otimes h$, invariance and symmetry of $B$ make the three factors $B([x,y],z)$, $B([y,z],x)$, and $B([z,x],y)$ equal. The cyclic cocycle sum is therefore that common factor times
$$\operatorname{Res}\bigl(((fq)'h+(qh)'f+(hf)'q)\,dt\bigr)=2\operatorname{Res}((fqh)'\,dt)=0.$$
Trilinearity extends the identity to all loop-algebra elements. Thus the terminology “two-cocycle” records a proved property of the defined form, not merely an intended later use.

For any long root $\alpha$, opposite root vectors normalized by $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=\alpha^\vee$ satisfy
$$B(e_\alpha,f_\alpha)=\frac{2}{(\alpha,\alpha)}=1.$$
The equality follows by pairing $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]$ with the Cartan and using invariance. A later result identifies the highest root and proves that it is long; no highest-root existence claim is used here.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with the invariant form used in [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]]. A representation $\rho$ of the loop central extension $\overline{L\mathfrak g}$ is a **restricted affine-current module of level $k\in\mathbb C$** if the central generator acts as $k\operatorname{id}$ and, for every vector $v$ and current $x\in\mathfrak g$, there is an integer $N(v,x)$ such that $\rho(x\otimes t^n)v=0$ for all $n\ge N(v,x)$.

The algebra in this definition is the central extension only; it does not contain the degree derivation. Restrictedness is a mode-truncation condition and does not itself supply an energy grading. A compatible positive-energy grading is extra structure on this current algebra.

derivations.claim: Choose a $B$-orthonormal complex basis $(e_a)$. Such a basis exists by finite-dimensional diagonalization: a nonzero symmetric nondegenerate form has a vector of nonzero square (otherwise polarization makes it zero), rescale that vector using a square root in $\mathbb C$, and induct on its nondegenerate orthogonal complement. Invariance gives $\sum_a([x,e_a]\otimes e_a+e_a\otimes[x,e_a])=0$: in this basis the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is skew-symmetric, since $B([x,u],v)=-B(u,[x,v])$. Also $\sum_a[e_a,[e_a,x]]=2h^\vee x$ by [F3]. This choice concerns only $\mathfrak g$, not an inner product on $V$.

Fix $v\in V$ and integers $m,n$. Expand $[J_x(n),T_m]$ by the product rule in the original normal order. All terms are finite on $v$: for $r\to+\infty$ the rightmost current or its commutator has index $r$ or $r+n$, and for $r\to-\infty$ it has index $m-r$ or $m-r+n$. These kill $v$ beyond a common bound, using [F5] for the finite family $e_a,[x,e_a]$. To identify the expansion with the commutator, the original truncated quadratic sum also stabilizes on both $v$ and $J_x(n)v$ by [F1]. Thus a sufficiently large cutoff gives the actual commutator, and all following identities are identities of eventually constant finite sums on $v$. Each factor contributes $nkJ_x(m+n)/2$ from the central term in [F2], by $\sum_aB(x,e_a)e_a=x$; their sum is $nkJ_x(m+n)$. This includes coincident indices: the two product-rule contributions are both retained.

Write $p=m+n$, $A_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_aJ_{[x,e_a]}(\alpha)J_{e_a}(\beta)$ and $D_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_aJ_{e_a}(\alpha)J_{[x,e_a]}(\beta)$ for $\alpha+\beta=p$. The noncentral expansion in step 2.1 is $\sum_{\alpha+\beta=p}(a_{\alpha,\beta}A_{\alpha,\beta}+b_{\alpha,\beta}D_{\alpha,\beta})$, with $$a_{\alpha,\beta}=\tfrac12(\mathbf1_{\alpha<n}+\mathbf1_{\beta\ge0}),\qquad b_{\alpha,\beta}=\tfrac12(\mathbf1_{\alpha<0}+\mathbf1_{\beta\ge n}).$$ Indeed the first normal-order half $r<0$ contributes $A$ at $\alpha=r+n<n$ and $D$ at $\alpha=r<0$; the reversed half $r\ge0$ contributes $A$ at $\beta=r\ge0$ and $D$ at $\beta=r+n\ge n$. The invariant tensor of step 1.1 gives $D_{\alpha,\beta}=-A_{\alpha,\beta}$. Set $f_n(j)=\mathbf1_{j<n}-\mathbf1_{j<0}$. Then $a-b=(f_n(\alpha)+f_n(\beta))/2$. Cancellation leaves a finite sum, since $f_n$ is supported on $0\le j<n$ for $n>0$, on $n\le j<0$ with value $-1$ for $n<0$, and is zero for $n=0$. The uncancelled tails before this cancellation are legitimate too: for $\alpha$ sufficiently negative the rightmost index $\beta$ is sufficiently positive, and for $\alpha$ sufficiently positive both coefficients are zero.

Exchange $\alpha,\beta$ in the term with coefficient $f_n(\beta)$. By the same invariant tensor, $A_{\beta,\alpha}=-\sum_aJ_{e_a}(\beta)J_{[x,e_a]}(\alpha)$. Hence the noncentral part is $$\frac12\sum_{\alpha+\beta=p}f_n(\alpha)\sum_a[J_{[x,e_a]}(\alpha),J_{e_a}(\beta)].$$ Here $B([x,e_a],e_a)=B(x,[e_a,e_a])=0$, so there is no additional central term. Moreover $\sum_a\bigl[\,[x,e_a],e_a\bigr]=\sum_a[e_a,[e_a,x]]=2h^\vee x$. As $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb Z}f_n(\alpha)=n$, including $n=0$ and negative $n$, [F2] reduces the displayed finite sum to $nh^\vee J_x(p)$. Together with step 2.1, this gives $[J_x(n),T_m]=n(k+h^\vee)J_x(p)$. Divide by $q\ne0$ and reverse the commutator to obtain the claim.

boundaries.evidence: For V=0 every endomorphism identity holds. The finite support of f_n cancels the formal infinite tails in 3.1.
At n=0, f_0=0 and both sides of [L_m,J_x(0)]=0 vanish (3.1–4.1). Level zero is allowed, critical level excluded.
At n=1, f_1 is the indicator of {0}, and the formula gives the previous mode-one commutator without positivity hypotheses.

boundaries.reason: B must be nondegenerate and q=k+h-dual nonzero, although the module needs no inner product.

boundaries.evidence: For n>0 the correction support is 0<=j<n, for n<0 it is n<=j<0 with sign -1. These include all zero-index endpoints (3.1).
The proof chooses one finite B-orthonormal basis by diagonalization, then uses finite cutoffs for e_a and [x,e_a] on each vector (1.1–2.1).
